source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CloudHQ's LC8 campus in Ashburn is published at 756 MW of IT capacity and 850,000 square feet of technical space. Those are the only two performance figures the operator puts on the page. The 756 MW is the largest published figure this site has read for any facility in Virginia, and it is roughly 29 percent of the 2,563.4 MW of published capacity across the 29 Virginia facilities that publish a number at all. That share is a statement about disclosure as much as about size, because 376 Virginia facilities are mapped and only 29 of them publish a megawatt figure.

The square footage and the megawatt figure together imply a density, and the density is the part that matters for AI. At 850,000 square feet of technical space and 756 MW, the campus works out to about 889 watts per square foot, which is far above a conventional enterprise data center and consistent with dense, power-hungry compute. To translate the power into racks, an assumption is required, and the operator does not publish one. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 756 MW of IT load is roughly 18,900 racks. At 100 kW per rack, a newer high-density figure, the same load is roughly 7,560 racks. Neither number is CloudHQ's claim, and the accelerator count depends on how many chips sit in each rack, which is not published.

The published specifications do not include certifications, so there is nothing here to read for what the campus is qualified to host. What the page does establish is a single site with more published power than any other in Virginia, in a state where published capacity is concentrated in a small minority of mapped facilities. For a reader asking whether this campus matters to AI, the answer is that it is the largest disclosed power block in the largest data center market in the country, and the grid connection behind those 756 MW is the constraint that determines when, or whether, the capacity is usable.
